questions.question: After a contained ransomware outbreak at a furniture maker, a department head wants the lessons learned review to focus on the technician who missed a patch. Which approach is BEST for the incident response lead?

options.A: Name the technician as the root cause in the review's findings
options.B: Cancel the review, since the incident was contained within hours
options.C: Find why one missed patch went unnoticed and assign owned fixes
options.D: Make retraining that technician the review's main corrective action

questions.key_concept: Lessons learned reviews are blameless: they look for process, tool and training gaps and give each fix an owner.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the review is for: finding someone to blame, or stopping the next incident. Then judge each option.
questions.correct_explanation: A lessons learned review is blameless: it asks why one missed patch could go unnoticed, such as gaps in patch tracking, asset records or monitoring, and gives each fix an owner and a deadline. Retraining the technician is the runner-up: skills matter, but it treats one person as the whole problem and leaves open the gaps that let a single miss cause an outbreak.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the missed patch let the attack in. But naming individuals makes people hide mistakes, and the real causes usually lie in process and controls.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the incident ended quickly. But small incidents still expose gaps, and reviewing them costs less than learning the same lesson from a bigger one.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: training can prevent repeat misses. But focusing on one person leaves the tracking and monitoring gaps that let one missed patch go unnoticed.

tips: Eliminate: A pins the cause on one person, which discourages honest reporting, and B skips a review because the incident was small.
Final two: C beats D because a review fixes the system that let one miss go unnoticed; retraining one person leaves those gaps open.
Exam cue: lessons learned reviews are blameless and end with owned, dated actions on process, tools and training.

questions.question: A hospital's incident response lead wants to confirm on-call responders can actually carry out the ransomware playbook's isolation steps within 30 minutes, without touching live systems. Which exercise fits this goal BEST?

options.A: A tabletop exercise in which the team talks through the steps
options.B: A functional exercise performing the steps on a simulated network
options.C: A drill in which staff phone everyone on the contact list
options.D: A read-through of the written ransomware playbook by the team

questions.key_concept: Tabletop exercises test roles and decisions by discussion; proving people can perform steps in time needs a hands-on functional exercise.
questions.pre_read: Notice what must be shown: people performing steps, and a time limit. Ask which exercises have people act rather than talk.
questions.correct_explanation: Only a hands-on exercise shows whether responders can perform the isolation steps and how long they take. In a functional exercise, responders carry out their roles in a simulated environment, so the time is measured without touching live systems. The tabletop is the runner-up: it is the best-known exercise and checks roles and decisions, but it is discussion only, so no step is performed or timed.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a tabletop checks who does what. But it is discussion only; nobody performs the steps, so it cannot show they take under 30 minutes.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because drills are hands-on. But calling the contact list tests whether people can be reached, not whether they can isolate systems.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the playbook must be right. But reading it checks the document, not whether responders can carry out its steps in time.

tips: Eliminate: C practices a different task, and D checks a document; neither has responders perform the isolation steps or measures time.
Final two: B beats A because a tabletop only discusses the steps; a functional exercise has responders perform and time them.
Exam cue: talk-through exercises test roles and decisions. To prove people can act within a time, choose a hands-on exercise.

questions.question: Midway through a weeks-long incident, a junior analyst finds that a detection rule missed the attacker's first step. Under NIST SP 800-61r3, what is the BEST way to handle this lesson?

options.A: Share it now with the detection team through the response lead
options.B: Hold it for the lessons learned meeting once recovery ends
options.C: Record it as the incident's root cause and close the analysis
options.D: Fix the detection rule themselves straight away in the live system

questions.key_concept: NIST's CSF 2.0-based model treats improvement as continuous: lessons are shared when found, not only after recovery.
questions.pre_read: Notice when the lesson appears and how long the incident has left to run. Then ask when it should reach its owner.
questions.correct_explanation: Current NIST guidance treats improvement as continuous: lessons should be shared as soon as they are found, not held until recovery ends. A detection gap could hide the attacker's next move, so passing it to the detection team through the response lead helps now. Holding it for the final meeting is the runner-up: that is the older model's timing, and the gap would stay open for weeks.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the older lifecycle collected lessons at the end. But current NIST guidance shares lessons as soon as they are found, and this gap matters now.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the miss feels central. But a missed detection explains why the attack went unseen, not how it got in, and analysis is still under way.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a quick fix seems helpful. But detection rules belong to their owners and change through approval; an unreviewed edit could break other detections.

tips: Eliminate: C mistakes a detection gap for the root cause and ends analysis early, and D changes another team's rule without approval.
Final two: A beats B because CSF 2.0-based guidance shares lessons when found; waiting leaves the gap open for weeks.
Exam cue: under CSF 2.0, improvement never stops. Share a lesson through the right owner as soon as you find it.

questions.question: A staff email account at a print shop is sending phishing messages to coworkers, and the playbook lets the on-call analyst disable accounts that send malicious mail. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Email all staff, warning them not to open the messages
options.B: Disable the email service for everyone until the investigation ends
options.C: Delete the phishing messages it sent from every coworker's mailbox
options.D: Disable the account that is sending the phishing messages

questions.key_concept: Containment stops the spread at its source first; clean-up and eradication follow under the incident response lead.
questions.pre_read: Find the source of the spread and what the playbook lets the analyst do. Then pick the step that stops the source.
questions.correct_explanation: Containment comes first, and the playbook gives the analyst authority to disable accounts, so disabling the sending account stops new phishing at its source; the incident response lead then directs the rest. Deleting the messages is the runner-up: it cleans up what was already sent, but the account keeps sending more while it stays active.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because warning people feels protective. But the account keeps sending, and incident messages to all staff come from the roles the plan names.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it would stop all phishing at once. But it halts every user's email when one account is the problem, a decision for management.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: removing the messages protects coworkers. But it is clean-up, not containment; while the account stays active, it keeps sending new ones.

tips: Eliminate: A warns staff while the source keeps sending, and B shuts down everyone's email, which is wider than needed and not the analyst's call.
Final two: D beats C because containment stops the source; deleting messages cleans up while new ones keep arriving.
Exam cue: contain before you clean up. When the playbook gives you the containment step, take it and report at once.

questions.question: A marketing team pays for an outside AI image service with a company card and uploads product photos to it. Which step is BEST for the IT asset analyst who learns of it?

options.A: Block the AI service's website at the web proxy straight away
options.B: Leave it out, since the inventory tracks company-owned hardware only
options.C: Add the AI service to the inventory and confirm its business owner
options.D: Let the provider track it, since the provider owns the systems

questions.key_concept: Asset inventories include outside services and AI tools, each with a named owner; unknown assets are recorded before any removal decision.
questions.pre_read: Ask what belongs in an asset inventory and who decides what happens to an asset. Then judge each option.
questions.correct_explanation: An inventory covers every asset the organization relies on, including outside services and AI tools, and each needs a named owner who is accountable for its use. Recording the service and confirming its owner brings it under management, so the owner can take it through the AI approval route. Blocking it is the runner-up: unknown services are a risk, but blocking is decided through the AI approval route, not by an analyst acting alone.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: unapproved services carry risk. But blocking a service the business relies on is decided through the AI approval route, not by an asset analyst alone.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because hardware is the classic inventory. But inventories also cover software, outside services and AI tools, or unknown services go unmanaged.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the provider runs the service. But the provider does not know what the organization uploads; tracking its own use stays with the organization.

tips: Eliminate: B limits the inventory to hardware, and D hands tracking to the provider; inventories cover the services and AI tools the organization uses.
Final two: C beats A because unknown assets are recorded and given an owner first; blocking is decided through the approval route, not by a lone analyst.
Exam cue: found something unknown? Record it and find its owner, who takes it through approval, before anyone blocks, unplugs or ignores it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-04 (inventories of services provided by suppliers are maintained); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 1.6 (mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems)

questions.question: A hotel group's procurement team will buy 300 smart room thermostats next month and plans to involve IT security after installation. What should the IT security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Set purchase requirements, such as patch support, before buying
options.B: Harden each thermostat to the secure baseline once it is installed
options.C: Pick the cheapest model and replace any that later prove insecure
options.D: Keep each thermostat's default settings, since the vendor is reputable

questions.key_concept: Security requirements, such as vendor patch support, belong in the acquisition stage, before any model is chosen.
questions.pre_read: Notice when IT security is due to get involved. Ask what can still be changed after the devices are bought.
questions.correct_explanation: Security belongs in the asset lifecycle from acquisition: requirements such as ongoing patch support, changeable default passwords and encryption should decide which model is bought. Hardening after installation is the runner-up: it is good practice, but it cannot add patch support or settings a model lacks, so 300 weak devices could be locked in for years.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: hardening to a baseline is good practice. But it cannot add patch support or settings a model lacks; those must be required before purchase.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it saves money now. But replacing insecure devices later costs more and leaves weak devices on the network until then.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reputable vendors seem trustworthy. But default settings favor easy setup over security and often include shared default passwords.

tips: Eliminate: C buys first and fixes later, and D trusts vendor defaults, which favor easy setup over security.
Final two: A beats B because hardening cannot add what a model lacks; requirements must shape the purchase.
Exam cue: security starts at acquisition. Requirements set before buying cost less than fixes after installation.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-4 (Acquisition Process); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-08 (systems, hardware, software, services, and data are managed throughout their life cycles)

questions.question: A drift scan flags that 15 file servers now run a backup agent missing from their secure baseline, and an approved change request installed it last week. What is the system administrator's BEST next step?

options.A: Remove the agent from all 15 servers to match the baseline again
options.B: Update the baseline through change management to add the agent
options.C: Turn off drift scanning on those servers to stop the repeat alerts
options.D: Report the agent as an unauthorized change and possible incident

questions.key_concept: Baselines change only through change management; an approved change that adds a component means the baseline must be updated.
questions.pre_read: Check whether the difference from the baseline was approved. Then ask which record is now out of date.
questions.correct_explanation: Drift is a difference from the baseline, but this one came from an approved change, so the baseline itself is now out of date. Updating it through change management makes it match the approved state, so future scans and new builds include the agent. Removing the agent is the runner-up: it restores the old baseline, but it undoes an approved change and stops the backups it provides.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: returning drift to the baseline is the usual fix. But this difference was approved; removing it undoes a sanctioned change and stops the backups.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the alerts are noise right now. But switching off drift checks hides every future change on those servers, approved or not.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because unapproved changes are treated as possible incidents. But this change has an approved request, so it is not unauthorized.

tips: Eliminate: C blinds the drift check, and D treats a change with an approved request as unauthorized.
Final two: B beats A because an approved change means the baseline is stale; update the baseline instead of undoing the change.

Exam cue: for any drift, ask first whether it was approved. Approved changes update the baseline; unapproved ones are restored by the system's maintainer, or reported as possible incidents when unexplained and risky.

questions.question: A security analyst's weekly review finds a new firewall rule, with no change request, allowing internet access to the payroll database on a firewall the network team runs. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Delete the rule at once to restore the approved configuration
options.B: File a change request now so the rule is approved retroactively
options.C: Leave it, since a senior engineer probably added it for a reason
options.D: Report it as a possible incident for responders to handle

questions.key_concept: An unexplained change that opens a serious exposure is a possible incident; if you do not run the system, report it instead of undoing it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an unexplained change could mean, and who runs the firewall. Then decide what the analyst's role allows.
questions.correct_explanation: A change with no approval is treated as a possible incident until explained, and a rule opening the payroll database to the internet could be an intruder's work. Reporting it starts the response, and the firewall's owners and responders decide on containment. Deleting the rule is the runner-up: it closes the exposure, but the analyst does not run the firewall, and deleting it alters the evidence responders need to trace who added it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the rule is risky and should not stay. But the network team runs the firewall, and deleting the rule alone alters evidence responders need to trace it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because change requests fix missing paperwork. But approving an unexplained rule after the fact could legitimize an intruder's change.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because senior staff do make quick fixes. But unapproved changes are treated as possible incidents until explained, whoever may have made them.

tips: Eliminate: B approves an unexplained change after the fact, and C assumes good intent without checking.
Final two: D beats A because an unexplained rule exposing payroll data is a possible incident, on a firewall the analyst doesn't run; owners and responders decide containment.
Exam cue: an unexplained change that opens a path to sensitive data is a possible incident. On a system you don't run, report it; don't quietly undo it.

questions.question: During threat modeling of a ticket-booking app, a junior analyst notes that a user could edit the price field in a request before it reaches the server. Which STRIDE category does this MOST accurately fit?

options.A: Spoofing, since the user poses as someone else
options.B: Tampering, since data is changed without permission
options.C: Repudiation, since the user could later deny the change
options.D: Elevation of privilege, since the user gains extra rights

questions.key_concept: STRIDE names six threat types; changing data without permission is tampering, a threat to integrity.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the user actually changes: their identity, their rights or the data. Then match it to a category.
questions.correct_explanation: Tampering is changing data or code without permission, a threat to integrity, and editing the price in a request is exactly that; the design fix is for the server to set or check prices itself. Elevation of privilege is the runner-up because the user gets a better deal, but their rights never change: they act as the same ordinary customer.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because attackers often fake identities. But the user acts as themselves; nothing here involves posing as another person or system.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because disputes over prices can follow. But repudiation is denying an action when there is no proof; the threat here is the changed data itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the user gains an advantage. But their rights stay the same; changing a value they should not control is tampering with data.

tips: Eliminate: A needs someone posing as another identity, and C is about denying actions later; neither describes an edited price.
Final two: B beats D because the user's rights never change; they alter data, which is tampering.
Exam cue: in STRIDE, ask what is violated: identity, data, proof of actions, secrecy, uptime or rights.

questions.question: During a tailgating test the client approved at a garden-supply wholesaler, a staff member grabs the arm of the tester posing as a courier, and others gather angrily. What should the tester do FIRST?

options.A: Keep up the courier story to see whether staff follow procedure
options.B: Ask to be walked to reception, still posing as the delivery courier
options.C: Stop the test, say who they are and show the authorization letter
options.D: End the test by pulling free and leaving by the nearest exit

questions.key_concept: Physical testers stop when anyone's safety is at risk and use their authorization letter so staff can verify the test.
questions.pre_read: Notice what has just changed in the situation. Then ask what matters more than finishing the test.
questions.correct_explanation: People's safety outranks any test result, so once a confrontation turns physical, the tester stops, identifies themselves and shows the signed authorization letter, which names a contact staff can call to verify it. Leaving at once is the runner-up: it ends the pretext, but pulling free can escalate a struggle, and staff are left believing a real intruder escaped.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the test is meant to be realistic. But realism never outweighs safety; once someone grabs the tester, the test has to stop.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reception is a calmer place. But keeping the pretext while staff are angry prolongs the danger; the letter exists for this moment.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it ends the confrontation quickly. But pulling free can turn into a struggle, and staff may chase or call police, believing a real intruder got away.

tips: Eliminate: A and B both keep the pretext going after the confrontation turned physical, when safety should end the test.
Final two: C beats D because revealing the role and letter calms the situation; fleeing can escalate it and leaves staff alarmed.
Exam cue: people come first. In any test or response, stop when someone could be hurt, and use the agreed way to verify.

questions.subtopic: 5.5 Security testing. Scanning and penetration testing
questions.question: A database owner approved monthly vulnerability scans, and the latest one flags a critical flaw that a junior analyst wants to exploit to prove it is real. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Get the owner's written approval and scope for a penetration test
options.B: Exploit it now, since the owner already approved the monthly scanning
options.C: Patch the flaw right away, since the scan rated it critical
options.D: Treat it as a false positive unless a second scanner agrees

questions.key_concept: Scanning and exploitation are different activities; each needs the system owner's approval for that type and level of testing.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the owner approved with what the analyst now wants to do. Ask whether one covers the other.
questions.correct_explanation: A scan identifies known weaknesses; exploiting one is penetration testing, which needs separate written approval and agreed scope from the system owner. Asking also tells the owner about the critical flaw. Exploiting under the scanning approval is the runner-up: it seems covered, but approval is for a specific type and level of testing, and an exploit can crash a production database.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the owner did approve testing of a kind. But scanning looks for flaws, and exploiting one is a different, riskier activity the approval does not cover.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because critical flaws need fixing fast. But the database belongs to its owner, and changing it skips change management; report the finding and let the owner decide.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because scanners do produce false positives. But a critical finding is validated and reported to the owner, not dismissed for lack of a second tool.

tips: Eliminate: C changes the owner's database without change management, and D dismisses a critical finding instead of validating and reporting it.
Final two: A beats B because approval covers a type and level of testing; scanning approval does not cover exploitation.
Exam cue: a scan finds weaknesses; a penetration test exploits them. Each needs the owner's approval for that specific activity.

questions.question: An authorized test shows a crafted message tricks a customer help desk chatbot into revealing internal staff phone numbers that customers never get. Which fix should the security analyst propose as BEST before retesting?

options.A: Add 'never reveal internal data' to the chatbot's instructions
options.B: Retrain the chatbot on a larger set of help desk chats
options.C: Accept the finding, since phone numbers are rarely sensitive data
options.D: Remove the chatbot's access to data it does not need

questions.key_concept: Models stay open to prompt injection, so limit the data and actions an AI tool can reach instead of relying on instructions.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the chatbot could be tricked again after each fix. Then pick the fix that still works if it is.
questions.correct_explanation: Current models remain open to prompt injection, so the strongest fix assumes the chatbot can be tricked and limits what it can reach: if it cannot access staff numbers, no message can extract them. Adding a 'never reveal' instruction is the runner-up: it may block some attempts, but instructions share the input stream attackers manipulate, and crafted messages often override them.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: clear instructions can block some attempts. But attackers craft input to override instructions, so the data stays reachable whenever a trick succeeds.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because more training sounds like better behavior. But extra help desk chats do not teach the model to resist crafted attacks, and the data stays reachable.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because phone numbers seem low risk. But internal contact lists fuel phishing, and accepting a risk is the owner's decision, not the analyst's.

tips: Eliminate: B adds training data that does nothing against manipulation, and C accepts a risk the analyst does not own.
Final two: D beats A because a chatbot that cannot reach the data cannot leak it; instructions can be talked around.
Exam cue: assume an AI tool can be tricked. Limit what it can access and do, then retest.
